newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour sees no new curbs on Murdoch media power.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour sees no new curbs on Murdoch media power.

text.p: British opposition Labour leader Tony Blair has said media tycoon Rupert Murdoch must exercise his power responsibly but Labour had no plans to curb his media interests if it wins power.
"It's not a question of Murdoch being too powerful," Blair said in an interview published on Thursday.
"He's got a strong position and whatever authority or power he has needs to be exercised responsibly," the left-leaning New Statesman weekly quoted Blair as saying.
"I would like to see a situation where that happens, not by legislation, but that people get a fair crack of the whip in the media," he added.
Opinion polls indicate that the centre-left Labour party is set to win the May 1 election, ending 18 years of Conservative rule.
Labour's prospects were boosted this week when the Murdoch-owned Sun, Britain's top-selling tabloid, announced that it was endorsing Blair.
The Sun, which has a daily circulation of four million copies, was fiercely critical of Labour and its former leader Neil Kinnock during the last election in 1992.

Murdoch's News International, the British arm of his News Corp company, accounts for around 35 percent of British newspaper sales. Its titles include The Sun and The Times dailies plus the Sunday Times and its fellow weekly News of the World.
It also owns 40 percent of British Sky Broadcasting Plc, the dominant force in British pay television.
Relations between Murdoch and the Labour party were soured in the 1980s when News International defeated the London print unions in a battle over introducing new technology.
Blair, a moderate who became party leader three years ago, has tried to build bridges with Murdoch, making a controversial trip to Australia to address News Corp executives in 1995.
Labour has denied that it has done any kind of deal with Murdoch in return for the Sun's support.

Media ownership legislation was passed last year and the issue is not likely to be high profile in the election. The law prevents newspaper groups with over 20 percent of national circulation from owning commercial terrestrial television companies.
